title: Does adoption spread through village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed?
summary: Research programme on the 43 Karnataka village networks of Banerjee, Chandrasekhar, Duflo and Jackson (2013; CC0 replication data, 9,126 households, 44,367 ties): can cross-sectional adoption data tell a simple contagion from a complex one, and which seeding rule stays near the best under every model the data cannot reject? Milestone 1 ports the authors’ estimation code (information model, five moments, identity weights, their 31 × 39 grid, Bayesian bootstrap). It reproduces the data (non-leader take-up 18.7% vs 18.5% published, leaders 24.7% vs 24.8%), q<sub>P</sub> > q<sub>N</sub> (98.4% of 1,000 bootstrap draws) and the counterfactual (take-up falls by 0.337 with non-adopters silent; paper 0.32), but not the published point: the minimum is q<sub>N</sub> = 0.05, q<sub>P</sub> = 0.30 for three seeds against 0.10, 0.50, which scores 11 times our minimum; q<sub>P</sub> is weakly identified (95% interval 0.15–1.0) and moves to 0.15–0.25 with two-step weights or quarterly periods. Milestone 2 fits two complex-contagion models on the same information spread, a reinforcement model (logit gains γ per adopting neighbour) and a fractional threshold, and compares them leaving one village out. Both fit better in sample (reinforcement γ = 0.10, positive in 99.5% of 1,000 bootstrap draws, criterion 41% lower; this fine-grid, free-intercept fit is post hoc, the pre-registered coarse grid gave γ = 0) yet predict held-out villages worse than the simple model (better in 13 and 19 of 43; in 12% and 24% of paired bootstrap draws). Take-up by adopting neighbours, 8.3% with none to 35.0% with four or more, is more convex than the simple model's 8.1% to 27.2%, a shape reinforcement, homophily or degree could each leave. Milestone 3 simulates 200 datasets from each fitted model on the real networks and refits all three: in sample the criterion picks the reinforcement model for 85% of datasets the simple model made; leaving one village out recovers the true model 58.5%, 82% and 55.5% of the time (simple, threshold, reinforcement), so milestone 2’s verdict is weak evidence. The moment map’s weakest direction trades the base adoption rate against word of mouth and reinforcement (condition number 79). A post-hoc check finds the real villages’ held-out errors two to four times larger than any model produces in its own synthetic data: every model is too homogeneous across villages. Milestone 3b adds a village random effect on the base adoption rate, identified by the squared village take-up rate: it is not needed (σ-hat = 0 in every family; the information model’s own word-of-mouth randomness already matches how much take-up varies between villages) and it does not close the gap (no synthetic dataset from the information or reinforcement model reaches the real held-out error). A threshold model with a free intercept does reach it (19% of its synthetic datasets) and now predicts held-out villages best (loss 0.169 against 0.181 and 0.210). The misfit is in where adopters sit, not how many: 57% of the real error is one moment, own adoption times second-neighbour adopters (a quirk of the original code), which a cascade model reproduces and a per-household-chance model cannot. Milestone 4 scores ten seeding rules at the leaders’ budget under all three fitted models: the advice barely depends on which model is right. Greedy seeding under the threshold model loses at most 0.5% of adopters against the best rule under every model (minimax-regret in 94% of bootstrap draws), the structural rules rank almost identically (Kendall τ 0.81–1.0), top degree loses 2–4%, the lender’s leaders 6–10%. Clustered seeds do not help even under the threshold model: one clustered patch is about as bad as random, and the best seeds have moderate degree and are rarely neighbours. Point fits, a fixed budget and no homophily; a model’s counterfactual, not a field result.
lede: research programme: does adoption spread through real village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed? On the 43 Banerjee et al. (2013) microfinance villages, the data cannot reliably tell the models apart, but the seeding advice survives that: one rule loses at most 0.5% of adopters under every fitted model, top-degree seeds lose 2 to 4%, the lender's leaders 6 to 10%, and clustering seeds together does not help.
